title: Joint Commission do not use abbreviations: how nurses spot them on Mac, 2026
metaTitle: Joint Commission do not use abbreviations: a Mac guide for nurses
description: Learn to spot prohibited order abbreviations on your Mac. Check the current Do Not Use list, scan notes and labels, and fix the habit for free.
targetKeyword: Joint Commission do not use abbreviations

intro: The Joint Commission's Do Not Use list names abbreviations you should not write in medical orders or notes. To spot them, check the current list, then scan every order, label, and note before you sign. This page covers what the mistake costs, why it keeps happening, and what you can fix on your Mac today for free.
tldr: The Joint Commission Do Not Use list names abbreviations that should not appear in orders or notes. Check the current version before you rely on memory.
ISMP's 2024 list says every item on it has been involved in harmful or potentially harmful medication errors.
Search each item with Find (⌘F) before you sign. Spell check will not catch these forms.
Apple Text Replacements can type approved, spelled-out wording for you in most apps. Test each one first.
Lazur explains terms, points at settings and guides you through steps. It does not click for you or check your orders.

blocks.text: What the Joint Commission Do Not Use list asks of you

The Joint Commission's Do Not Use list names abbreviations you should not write in medical orders or notes. ISMP publishes a separate list of error-prone abbreviations, symbols, and dose designations. ISMP marks the items that also appear on the Joint Commission list. Knowing the list is only half the job. The other half is checking your own text before it leaves your hands.

ISMP released its 2024 list on April 18, 2024. The rule covers more than typed text. ISMP says its items should not appear in verbal, handwritten, or electronic communication. They also should not appear on medication labels, administration records, or order-entry or dispensing screens. That means a form that looks fine in a chart note can still fail on a label.

blocks.title: Use the current version
blocks.text: Lists change. ISMP's 2024 update changed several items, so a printout from before April 2024 can mislead you. Replace old copies with the current list, then date your cheat sheet.
What prohibited abbreviations cost patients and staff

Start with the largest figure you can source. WHO says the cost associated with medication errors has been estimated at $42 billion USD annually. The page does not name the year or the method behind that estimate. Treat it as an old, global figure. It does not isolate prohibited abbreviations, so do not quote it as a number for abbreviations.

WHO describes medication errors as causing severe harm, disability and even death. It sets a goal to reduce severe avoidable medication-related harm by 50% globally within five years. Clear written orders are one practical part of that goal. This page cannot tell you how much of that harm comes from abbreviations.

No verified source here gives a count of patients harmed by items on the ISMP list. ISMP says every item was reported through its voluntary error reporting program. It also says each item has been involved in harmful or potentially harmful medication errors. The page gives no error counts or rates. So the list tells you which forms are risky. It does not tell you how often they hurt someone on your unit.

Your own costs are harder to measure, and no verified figure exists for them. A clarification call takes time. A dose can wait while someone asks what an abbreviation means. An incident report takes more time still. For a week, keep a tally. Write down each call to ask what a term means. That gives you a number for your unit that no national study can give you.
Why prohibited abbreviations keep showing up

items: Paper habits carry over. Handwritten shorthand often ends up in typed notes, even when you know the rule.
Templates and copy-paste keep old text alive. A template built before ISMP's 2024 update may still hold older forms.
Channels follow different rules. A form that passes in a chart note can fail on a label or in a verbal order.
Spell check does not know the list. It checks spelling against dictionaries, not against a safety rule.
Busy shifts push you toward shortcuts. No source on this page measures that effect on a unit, so treat it as a common pattern.
Memory fills the gap. Once a term feels familiar, you stop checking the current list.

blocks.text: The 2024 update changed some items that experienced nurses still use. ISMP asks you to spell out nanog. It asks you to spell out intranasal instead of NAS. It asks you to use QHS instead of nightly or HS for bedtime. It also asks you to avoid reduced-size fractions for half tablets, and to use and instead of per as a slash.

blocks.text: Electronic order entry is one control that helps. In a 2014 systematic review of 16 studies, computerized provider order entry (CPOE) was linked to fewer medication errors than paper orders. The pooled risk ratio was 0.46, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.35 to 0.60. The authors called the study designs weak, and the results varied widely. Read that number as a direction, not a promise about your screen.
Check your notes for prohibited abbreviations, step by step

Use this routine before you sign, hand off, or print a label. A short note takes only a few minutes once the habit sticks. Keep the current list open in Chrome while you work, and keep your cheat sheet in Word.

items: Open the current ISMP list in Chrome and keep the tab open. Save a PDF copy with ⌘P for offline use.
Open your draft in Word, or the charting page in Chrome.
Press ⌘F and search for one item from your cheat sheet at a time.
Read each hit. Decide whether it sits in a dose, a label, a handoff, or a plain phrase.
Replace each prohibited form with the spelled-out term your facility approves.
Ask pharmacy or your charge nurse when a term is unclear. Do not guess.

blocks.text: Find only works on text you can see on the screen. It does not read scanned forms, photos, or handwriting. Check those by eye, against the same list.
Run the check again for labels and verbal orders. ISMP covers those channels too. A note that passes Find can still fail on a printed label.
Free fixes you can set up on your Mac today
You do not need to buy anything to start. Apple and Microsoft already include the tools you need. Start with two settings: Text Replacements in macOS, and the custom dictionary in Word.
Set up Text Replacements

Open Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements. Click Add. Type the short text you type and the full text it should become. Click Done. Apple's Mac Help says text replacements are not available in all apps, so test each app where you chart.

Pick triggers you never type by accident. For example, bedt could expand to at bedtime. Avoid triggers that match real words. Avoid any trigger that expands into a prohibited form. Test each shortcut once in Word and once in your charting app before you rely on it.
Teach Word your approved terms

Word checks spelling against dictionaries. If it flags an approved term such as intranasal, add that term to a custom dictionary. Go to Word > Preferences > Authoring and Proofing Tools > Spelling & Grammar > Dictionaries. Select the dictionary, click Edit, and add the word. Microsoft says this works in Word 2016 through Microsoft 365 for Mac.

Do not mistake the dictionary for a safety check. Adding a term only clears a red underline. It does not stop a prohibited form, which can be a real short string that spell check accepts without comment.
Set a quarterly list check

Open Apple Reminders and create a reminder titled Check the Do Not Use list. Set it to repeat every quarter. Put the ISMP link in the notes field. When it fires, check the publication date of each source and update your cheat sheet. An old printout can quietly mislead you for a long time.
Worked example: fixing a note line by line

Say your draft reads: NAS spray given nightly. Press ⌘F and search for NAS. The hit is a prohibited form, so replace it with intranasal. Search for nightly next. Replace it with QHS, as ISMP suggests, or with the spelled-out bedtime wording your facility approves. Your facility decides which of those goes into the final note. Read the line once more before you sign it.
Mistakes people make with prohibited abbreviations

items: Trusting memory. A term you learned years ago may have changed in the 2024 update.
Treating the list as the whole rule. Your facility policy can be stricter than the list. Follow the stricter rule.
Using spell check as a safety net. It checks spelling, not safety.
Forgetting the other channels. Verbal orders, handwritten notes, labels, and screens all count.
Swapping one abbreviation for another. Spell the term out unless your policy names a replacement.
Fixing a template once and forgetting it. Old templates bring back old forms.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold Option and Command to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app.

Use it for the parts that need a second pair of eyes or a faster hand. Ask what a term means while you chart, and Lazur answers from what it sees on screen. Ask where Text Replacements is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to add a shortcut, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. It does not check your notes against the Joint Commission list. Confirm each term against the current list and your facility policy.

blocks.title: Patient data comes first
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on patient data before you use any AI tool at work. Practice with sample or de-identified text. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Do not show it patient identifiers unless your employer allows it.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are Lazur's stated terms. They do not replace your employer's rules, and your facility can still say no. If it does, follow that answer.
Dictate and draft safer text without typing the banned forms

Dictation can help you write spelled-out text faster. Hold fn and speak. The text lands at the cursor in any app. Snippets and a personal dictionary can hold the approved wording, so you do not retype it each shift.

Read the dictated text after every run. Speech tools can mishear terms, and a word that sounds like a short code may come out wrong. Check each term that matters before you sign or send. Use drafts for generic text, such as your cheat sheet, not for patient notes unless your employer allows it.

faq.question: Where can I find the current Joint Commission Do Not Use list?
faq.answer: Start with The Joint Commission's own website and search for its Do Not Use list. Check the publication date on the page. Secondary websites disagree on some entries, so the primary source wins. Your facility policy sits on top of both lists.

faq.question: How is the ISMP list different from the Joint Commission list?
faq.answer: ISMP released its 2024 list on April 18, 2024. It marks the items that also appear on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list. ISMP also says its items should not appear in verbal, handwritten, or electronic communication, on labels, or on order-entry screens. Use both lists, then your facility policy.

faq.question: Does spell check catch prohibited abbreviations in Word?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Spell check compares words against dictionaries, not against a safety list. Use Find with your own cheat sheet. Add approved terms to a custom dictionary if spell check flags them, but treat that as tidying up, not as a safety check.

faq.question: Can Lazur check my notes for prohibited abbreviations?
faq.answer: Lazur can answer questions about what is on screen while you hold Option and Command. It is not a verified safety checker, and it does not check your notes against the Joint Commission list. Ask it what a term means, then confirm against the current list and your facility policy.

faq.question: Should I change old notes I wrote before the 2024 update?
faq.answer: This page does not give a rule for old records. Follow your facility's records policy. Change how you write from now on, and check the templates you still use. Ask your manager or pharmacy if you are unsure what applies.

faq.question: What if my unit has a stricter rule than the published list?
faq.answer: Follow the stricter rule. Your facility policy can be stricter than the Joint Commission list or the ISMP list. If your unit bans a form that appears on neither list, the unit rule still applies. Ask your manager when you are unsure.

faq.question: Is there a verified count of how often these abbreviations cause harm?
faq.answer: No. ISMP says each item has been involved in harmful or potentially harmful medication errors, but its page gives no counts or rates. Track your own clarification calls for a week. That gives you a local picture.

costs.title: Patient harm, in ISMP's words
costs.text: ISMP says every item on its list has been involved in harmful or potentially harmful medication errors. That is a risk statement, not a frequency. The page gives no counts or rates. Treat each form on the list as a known source of error, even if you have never seen it cause one.

costs.title: A global dollar figure, with caveats
costs.text: WHO estimates the cost of medication errors at $42 billion USD a year. The page gives no year and no method. Use it as a rough, old global number. It does not measure abbreviations on your unit, so do not quote it as a local cost.

costs.title: Your time and your unit's time
costs.text: A clarification call takes minutes. A delayed dose, a pharmacy callback, and an incident report take more. No verified source gives a number for these minutes on your unit. Count them for a week. That number helps your manager more than any national average.

costs.title: Your name is on the note
costs.text: The person who signs an order or note owns its wording. If an unclear abbreviation leads to a bad outcome, expect a review to ask what was written and who wrote it. Follow your facility's documentation policy, and expect questions about any term that is not on the approved list.

causes.title: Paper habits carry over
causes.text: Many nurses learned shorthand on paper charts and kept it. Handwritten habits often end up in typed notes, orders, and handoffs. The habit feels harmless because you know what you meant. The reader may not. ISMP's list covers handwritten communication for that reason.

causes.title: Templates and copy-paste keep old text alive
causes.text: A template built before ISMP's 2024 update can still contain older forms. Copy-paste carries the same problem from one note to the next. Each copy looks familiar, so nobody rechecks it. Review your templates every quarter, along with your own cheat sheet.

causes.title: Each channel follows its own rules
causes.text: ISMP says its items should not be used in verbal, handwritten, or electronic communication. They also should not appear on medication labels, on administration records, or on order-entry or dispensing screens. A form that passes in a chart note can still fail on a label. Check each channel you touch.

causes.title: Spell check gives false comfort
causes.text: Spell check compares words against dictionaries. It was not built to flag a clinical safety rule, so a prohibited form can pass without a warning. Many people assume a clean spell check means a clean note. That assumption is the gap this page is about.

causes.title: Fast shifts and interruptions
causes.text: A busy shift pushes you toward the shortest form that gets the message across. Interruptions make it harder to check a term before you move on. This page includes no source that measures how often this happens on a unit. Treat it as a common pattern, not a measured rate.

causes.title: Familiar terms outlast the current list
causes.text: Memory fills the gap between what you learned and what the list says now. The 2024 changes show how this happens. A term that was accepted for years can become a term to spell out. Only the current list catches that shift.

fixes.title: Pull the current lists yourself
fixes.text: Open ISMP's 2024 list in Chrome. ISMP released it on April 18, 2024. Save a PDF copy with ⌘P, then choose Save as PDF from the PDF menu. Check the Joint Commission Do Not Use list on The Joint Commission's own site. Check your facility policy last, because the stricter rule wins on your unit.

fixes.title: Keep one cheat sheet in Word
fixes.text: Make one document with a table. The left column holds the written form. The right column holds the approved wording. Start with the 2024 changes, then add items from your facility list. Keep patient information out of the file so it stays a reference, not a record.

fixes.title: Run a Find pass before you sign
fixes.text: Press ⌘F in Word or Chrome and search each item from your cheat sheet. Read every hit in context. Find cannot see handwriting, photos, or scanned forms, so check those by eye. Repeat the pass for labels and verbal orders, since the list covers those channels.

fixes.title: Use Text Replacements for approved wording
fixes.text: Open Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements. Map short triggers to the full approved phrase. Apple says text replacements are not available in all apps, so test each one in the app where you chart. Pick triggers that never match a real word.

fixes.title: Teach Word the approved terms
fixes.text: Add approved spelled-out terms to a Word custom dictionary, so spell check stops flagging them. Go to Word > Preferences > Authoring and Proofing Tools > Spelling & Grammar > Dictionaries. Adding a term only clears a red underline. It does not check safety.

fixes.title: Ask a person when a term is unclear
fixes.text: Pharmacy, your charge nurse, or your facility's medication safety team can answer, if your facility has one. Spelling out a term costs a few extra words. Guessing can cost much more. Write the term out in full and ask before you sign.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pull the current lists
plan.text: Open The Joint Commission's Do Not Use page and ISMP's 2024 list in Chrome. Save both as PDF with ⌘P. Write down the publication date on each. Ask your unit which facility policy overrides them.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Build your cheat sheet
plan.text: Make a table in Word with the written form on the left and the approved wording on the right. Start with the ISMP 2024 changes, including nanog, NAS, nightly, HS, the slash for per, and fractions for half tablets. Add the items from your facility list.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set up Text Replacements
plan.text: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements. Add shortcuts for phrases you type often, using triggers that never match a real word. Test each one in Word and in your charting app.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Scan a sample note
plan.text: Use a sample or de-identified note, not patient records, unless your employer approves the tool. Press ⌘F and search each cheat sheet item. Fix each hit, then read the sentence again.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set the review
plan.text: Create a repeating reminder in Apple Reminders for the list check each quarter. Put the ISMP link in the notes. When it fires, confirm the publication date and update your cheat sheet.
